messages.text: Will a power spike fry the whole miner?

Good question — and this is actually one of the Rev 6.1's real design wins.

**No. A spike hits the onboard F1 fuse first, not the electronics.**

Here's how it works:

- The board has a **dedicated F1 fuse** — a small automotive-style blade fuse sitting right next to the yellow XT30 power input
- A power spike blows **that fuse**, not the BM1370 chips or anything else behind it
- You replace a cheap sacrificial fuse instead of a $249 miner

**Why it matters:** cheaper home miners skip this protection entirely. A spike there cooks the whole board. Here it costs you a fuse.

The **XT30 connector** (also Rev 6.1's upgrade over the old 8A barrel jack) and the **thicker copper PCB** back this up — the whole power path is built to handle real sustained current without sagging or melting.

So: well-protected, not bulletproof — but the failure mode is "replace a fuse," not "buy a new miner."
Is it quiet enough to run in my office?

Yes, genuinely.

**~40–45 dB** is the honest range — that's quiet-room level, like a gentle fan or a library hum. Not silent, but absolutely desk-friendly.

A few reasons it stays that way:

- **One large front fan** running slow — big slow airflow beats a screaming tiny fan
- **Spring-mounted heatsink** presses evenly on all 4 BM1370 chips — no one hot die forcing the fan to spin up
- **~57 °C on the ASICs at full load** — it's not fighting heat, so the fan doesn't have to

**Size-wise:** ~20 × 11 × 5.8 cm, **0.5 kg** — palm-sized, sits on its 3D-printed stand angled toward you.

Plenty of people run these on a desk next to a monitor. If your office is already quiet enough to hear a laptop fan, you'll notice it — but it won't drive you out of the room.
